content.title: Kitchen Fitting Costs in London 2027: 7 Things Your Quote Should Explain
content.summary: Seven fitting work packages, a responsibility sheet and the distinction between installed cabinets and a usable kitchen.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Fitting Costs London 2027: 7 Quote Checks | NURA
content.seo_description: Comparing kitchen fitting costs in London? Check 7 parts of your 2027 quote, including labour, plumbing, electrics, removal and separately priced work.

hero.alt: Clay kitchen cabinetry with an island, pale worktop and grouped cabinet and finish samples
hero.caption: Cabinet, panel and surface choices need a clearly defined fitting scope. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Clay kitchen cabinetry with an island, pale worktop and grouped cabinet and finish samples
social_image.caption: Cabinet, panel and surface choices need a clearly defined fitting scope. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: Kitchen fitting costs in London are only comparable when the work behind each total is clear. For a 2027 project, ask for a current, site-specific quotation covering the seven areas below. Separate cabinet fitting from the work needed to make the room usable, and give every task a named responsibility. This is a scope guide, not a forecast of 2027 prices.
For context,
Checkatrade's kitchen fitting guide

, checked in October 2026, gives £2,000 to £6,000 for labour to fit a family kitchen, with £3,500 as its average. That is its UK benchmark for a described job, not a London average, a Nura price or a 2027 quotation. A price for cabinet installation alone and one covering several trades describe different commissions.
Use this guide when you have a layout and want to understand the fitting bill. For cabinet materials, hardware and the supplied specification, use the
bespoke kitchen quote comparison
. For the whole project budget, see
new kitchen costs in London
1. Removal, protection and access

Ask whether the price includes disconnecting the existing kitchen through the appropriate trades, removing units and worktops, carrying waste out and arranging disposal. Keep removal and disposal as separate questions: a stack of dismantled cabinets is not a cleared room.

Show the delivery and waste route, including stairs, lift restrictions and places where materials could be stored. Ask who prices parking, protection and any permissions needed for the proposed arrangements. Record which existing floors, doors or fittings must be retained. These details belong in the site assessment rather than an assumed London surcharge.
2. Cabinet assembly, fitting and visible panels

Attach the actual unit list and drawing revision. Ask whether assembly, positioning, fixing, door adjustment, handles, plinths, fillers and exposed ends are included. Identify any panels or trim supplied separately and who checks they have arrived before the relevant work starts.

An oak end panel beside painted doors is an aesthetic choice with installation consequences: the side, edge and junction with the wall need to be described, not left under a general heading of units. Agree what a finished cabinet run should look like. A fitting allowance cannot resolve an undecided panel detail.

body_nodes.alt: Clay tall cupboards with an oak end panel beside matching cabinet finish samples
body_nodes.caption: Visible ends and fillers deserve a place in the fitting scope alongside the cabinet list. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: 3. Plumbing and the usable sink

List the sink, tap, dishwasher and any other water-connected products by model. Ask which existing connections can be retained, what needs assessment and who prices alterations. Distinguish positioning an appliance from connecting it, checking it and leaving it usable.

If another contractor is doing the plumbing, name that responsibility on the same sheet. Ask what must be ready before the final connection visit and who arranges it. Do not assume that a fitted sink bowl means the kitchen has a working water supply and waste connection.
4. Electrics, gas and extraction

Give the relevant trades the appliance and lighting requirements, plus proposed positions. Ask for electrical alterations, final connections, extraction work and applicable testing or certification to be stated explicitly. The practical question is who assesses and prices each task, not whether a broad fitting label sounds comprehensive.
Gas work requires a Gas Safe registered engineer under
GOV.UK guidance
. Ask who is arranging that work where it applies. Do not treat moving a gas hob, changing an electrical appliance or choosing a new extractor as a cabinet-only decision. The
first-fix coordination guide
covers the wider sequence.
5. Worktops and separate visits

Record measurement or templating, fabrication, delivery, fitting, cut-outs and finishing as distinct tasks. Ask the chosen worktop supplier what must be ready before measurement and installation, and who confirms that readiness. The answer depends on the specified product and installation method.

Where the worktop and plumbing are separate commissions, identify who books the final connection after the surface is installed. Ask how a missed or additional visit would be priced. There is no useful universal return-visit allowance without the supplier's actual scope.
6. Walls, floors and decoration

Describe the intended finish beyond the cupboards: wall repairs, splashbacks, flooring edges, skirting and paint. Ask who assesses the substrate and who prices making good after removal or service alterations. Identify full-room work separately from local repairs.

If you want to retain a floor or splashback, show it in the brief and ask how the proposed work affects it. A new cabinet line can change what is visible. Agree how unresolved areas will be assessed before treating a repair allowance as a finished-room price.
7. Programme, changes and handover

Ask for the assumptions behind the programme, the person coordinating separate trades and the process for agreeing changes. Record the quotation's validity, payment stages, VAT presentation and any provisional amounts. Confirm how extra work and return visits are approved before they are commissioned.

Define handover in practical terms: the agreed work complete, identified defects recorded, applicable documents supplied and a contact for unresolved items. Separately ask when the sink and cooking appliances are expected to be usable. Cabinet fitting complete and kitchen usable may be different milestones; obtain the actual plan for your room.

body_nodes.alt: A pale kitchen worktop with a stainless steel sink, tap and open blank planning notebook
body_nodes.caption: Ask when the sink will be usable and which documents and checks belong at handover. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: Put the responsibilities on one sheet

For each row, add the written price reference, named contractor and status: included, separately quoted, allowance or unresolved. An unresolved task is not a zero-cost task. The examples below are questions to complete, not standard Nura contract inclusions.
Work package
Record before comparing totals
Removal and access
Who clears waste, protects retained finishes and prices access arrangements?
Cabinet fitting
Which units, panels, fillers and final adjustments are covered?
Plumbing
Who connects and checks each product, and what must be ready?
Electrics, gas and extraction
Who assesses, installs and supplies applicable documents?
Worktop visits
Who confirms readiness and arranges later connections?
Room finishes
Which repairs, flooring edges and decoration are included?
Programme and handover
Who coordinates, approves changes and resolves outstanding work?

Consider a hypothetical household that wants an oak side panel to finish a tall bank and needs a working sink before returning to normal cooking. The cabinet quote covers the panel, the surface supplier prices the worktop, and the plumbing responsibility is still unconfirmed. Their next step is to resolve the connection and readiness arrangements, rather than assuming the cabinet completion date answers both needs. No cost or completion date follows from this example.
Bring the unfinished decisions to Nura

Prepare room and access photographs, an annotated plan, unit and appliance lists, finish references and the responsibility sheet. Mark what you want to retain and the daily activity you most need the finished kitchen to support.
Explore a documented London kitchen
for design context, without assuming its fitting scope or cost applies to yours.
Discuss your kitchen brief with Nura
and ask which parts of the proposed scope can be included in its quotation. The
bespoke kitchen service
connects the design decisions; ask what material examples are available before arranging a
Fulham showroom visit

content.title: Kitchen Table Centrepieces That Make Way for Dinner
content.summary: Set out an ordinary meal before deciding whether the centrepiece stays on the table or moves elsewhere.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Table Centrepieces for Everyday Meals | NURA
content.seo_description: Choose a kitchen table centrepiece around your usual place settings, seated view and serving dishes, then decide whether it stays or moves for meals.

hero.alt: An oak kitchen table with four ivory place settings and a low empty ceramic vessel beside blue cabinetry
hero.caption: A low ceramic vessel joins the table setting and kitchen palette. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: An oak kitchen table with four ivory place settings and a low empty ceramic vessel beside blue cabinetry
social_image.caption: A low ceramic vessel joins the table setting and kitchen palette. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: A kitchen table centrepiece should work with the meal, not just the empty table. Start with your usual place settings and serving dishes, then try one object you already own. Decide whether it can stay while you eat or needs a clear place elsewhere. Either answer can lead to a table you enjoy using.
Set the table before choosing the decoration

Begin without a centrepiece. Put out the plates, glasses and empty serving dishes you use for an ordinary meal, in their usual positions. Notice which part of the middle you actually use. A display for a table where food is served from the kitchen can be different from one where everyone shares dishes at the table.

Try a single stable, dry, empty vase in the remaining space. Keep the whole base supported and follow the care guidance for your table and the object. You are rehearsing your own arrangement, not following a universal rule about how much of the tabletop to fill.
Look from the chair as well as the doorway

Sit in the seats you normally use and compare the view across the table with the view from the kitchen entrance. Notice whether the object interrupts a view you want to keep, or makes reaching your place setting awkward.
TLC Interiors' dining-table guide
also considers the seated view; your own table and chairs provide the useful comparison here.

body_nodes.alt: A seated view across an oak table with an empty ivory vessel, plates and a chair opposite
body_nodes.caption: The view across the table matters alongside the view into the room. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: There is no need to add stems immediately. Choose the vessel first; if you later add flowers or foliage, compare the complete arrangement again. Its outline will have changed.
Choose a stay-or-move arrangement

If the centrepiece competes with the serving dishes, try a smaller arrangement or remove it for meals. Identify a clear, stable place where it can stand, with its base fully supported. An occupied worktop or the floor is not a useful default destination.
Your usual meal

Plates arrive already served
Can the object stay without interrupting the seated view or everyday reach?

Does a smaller piece work, or will the decoration move before the table is set?

body_nodes.caption: A planned place off the table lets decoration make way for the meal. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

Keeping the vase on a nearby sideboard during dinner preserves the colour relationship without asking the meal to fit around it. Leaving the table clear is also a deliberate choice.

wood-tone guide
considers retained furniture, while the
fruit-bowl tip
addresses the bowl's changing contents.

. They help explain the relationship you want between cabinetry and the furniture you keep.

for context, and ask which relevant material examples are available before a

content.title: Will a Kitchen Island Fit? 5 Measurements That Shape a Better Layout
content.summary: Record the finished island, surrounding routes, occupied seats and open appliances on the same plan.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Island Dimensions: 5 Measurements to Plan | NURA
content.seo_description: Plan your kitchen island around 5 measurements: length, depth, walkways, seating space and appliance door clearance. Find out what works for your room.

hero.alt: Terracotta kitchen with a pale rectangular island, oak cabinetry and two timber seats seen from above
hero.caption: A finished island outline includes the worktop and the seating side. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Terracotta kitchen with a pale rectangular island, oak cabinetry and two timber seats seen from above
social_image.caption: A finished island outline includes the worktop and the seating side. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: A useful kitchen island plan records more than the cabinet size. Measure the finished length and depth, the space around it, the seating in use and the appliances fully open. Those five records help you compare an island with a smaller preparation block, a peninsula or a kitchen without one, before choosing its appearance.

Start with a measured room plan showing walls, openings, radiators and existing furniture. Use one unit throughout, such as millimetres, and distinguish confirmed site measurements from provisional furniture sizes. The illustrations here explain planning ideas; they are not measured layouts or construction drawings.
1. Finished length: include the ends you will actually see

Record the outside length of the proposed worktop, then identify what sits beneath it: cabinets, end panels, supports and any seating recess. A cabinet schedule alone does not describe the whole island. Compare the finished outline with the route past each end, including the way from the kitchen entrance to the dining table or garden.

Ask what the extra length earns. Is it another drawer, a clear preparation surface or a seat used every day? If it only extends a surface already large enough for your routine, compare a shorter version before reducing the surrounding space.
2. Finished depth: draw the worktop and cabinets separately

Measure across the finished island from one outside worktop edge to the other. Show the cabinet footprint beneath as a second outline. Back panels, storage on the reverse and a seating overhang can change the depth even when the front cabinet sizes stay the same.

Check how you will reach and clean the surface from the available sides. If the island includes seating, confirm the worktop support and overhang with the supplier for that exact material and detail. An attractive illustration cannot establish structural suitability or a universal unsupported overhang.

content.title: How Long Does a Kitchen Renovation Take in 2027? 7 Stages Explained
content.summary: Separate design and ordering, work on site and time without a usable kitchen through seven stages and a practical handover record.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Renovation Timeline 2027: 7 Stages | NURA
content.seo_description: Understand the 7 stages of a kitchen renovation in 2027, from design to final connections, and separate ordering lead times from time without a working kitchen.

hero.alt: Illustrated sequence from kitchen plans to cabinet installation and a finished blue and walnut kitchen
hero.caption: Planning, cabinet installation and the finished room represent different milestones. Illustration, Nura Interiors; no duration or actual project is depicted.

social_image.alt: Illustrated sequence from kitchen plans to cabinet installation and a finished blue and walnut kitchen

children.text: A kitchen renovation has no single reliable duration without a defined scope, specification and site assessment. If you are planning for 2027, separate three periods: design and ordering, work inside the home, and the time without a usable sink or cooking appliances. The year on the plan does not establish future product availability or a delivery promise.
For context, the
Federation of Master Builders

describes a basic like-for-like fitting as a matter of weeks, excluding planning; complex work can take longer. That is broad guidance, not a quotation for your room. Ask for a current written programme with a starting condition and a named person responsible for each handover.
1. Define the brief and the work around it

Record what you want to retain, what must change and how you use the kitchen. A cabinet replacement and a project involving building work need different assessments. Include access, existing services, adjacent rooms and any proposed structural changes in the conversation with the relevant professionals.

Write down your household priority. Returning to ordinary meals may depend on a working sink and oven, rather than the date the last door is adjusted. Give the coordinator both your preferred completion date and the daily functions you need back.
2. Resolve design and technical decisions

Bring the layout, appliance models, cabinet details and finish choices into the same drawing revision. Ask the appropriate professionals which surveys, permissions and technical decisions apply before work is commissioned. Do not assume every renovation needs the same approvals.

A hypothetical household might choose navy painted doors around a retained walnut table, while still debating the sink and worktop edge. Their colour direction is useful, but it does not resolve the sink specification. Record who needs that answer and which later tasks depend on it.

body_nodes.alt: Kitchen plan with navy door and walnut samples beside seven blank milestone cards
body_nodes.caption: Plans, finish references and separate milestone cards represent decisions to resolve. Illustration, Nura Interiors; no dated programme is shown.

children.text: 3. Confirm orders and readiness together
For each product, distinguish an enquiry, an accepted order, an expected dispatch and an agreed delivery. Ask what releases production and when the supplier will confirm the next milestone. Use the
lead-times guide
for those narrower supply questions.

Connect deliveries with a prepared room, suitable storage and someone responsible for receiving and checking the goods. Ask whether the existing kitchen can remain usable during some of this period. Ordering lead time should not automatically become time without a kitchen.
4. Agree removal, services and room preparation

Before removal, confirm the sequence with the appointed coordinator, including protection, disposal, service work and the assessment of anything exposed. Ask how discoveries will be reported and how changed work or dates will be agreed.

Flooring, plaster, decoration and cabinetry need a sequence suited to the selected systems and site conditions. Obtain the relevant readiness requirements rather than applying one universal order or drying allowance. The
first-fix guide
develops the service-coordination questions.
5. Treat fitted cabinets as a handover

Agree who checks the cabinet installation and confirms readiness for the next supplier. List the panels, fillers, openings and other details the following work depends on. Ask how missing or damaged components affect the next visit.

Cabinet installation is a visible milestone, but it does not by itself establish that the sink or cooking appliances are connected and usable. Keep those practical dates separate on the same programme.
6. Coordinate surfaces, finishes and connections
Ask the chosen worktop supplier when measurement or templating can happen, what must be ready and how fabrication and fitting will be booked.
Day True's own process
illustrates why worktop templating can follow fixed cabinetry; its durations and commercial terms are specific to that supplier.
Confirm who books the later plumbing, appliance and electrical work, and which tasks depend on the installed surface. Gas work requires
Gas Safe registration under GOV.UK guidance
. Ask the relevant trades about checks and applicable documentation. A surface in place is not proof that every connection is complete.

Agree what handover covers: operation of the specified products, applicable documents, care information and a written list of unresolved work with a responsible contact. Record usable-sink and cooking milestones explicitly, alongside final completion.

A drawer can bring its contents forward; a shelved cupboard offers a different arrangement of height and access. Matching the fabric only to the wooden tabletop can miss the point: a full cloth hides most of that wood. A runner leaves it in view, so the same colour choice becomes a different composition.
Start with what stays visible

content.summary: Compare the stored appliance with the movements, door positions and separate worktop needed around it, using each model's instructions.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Appliance Garage: Plan Beyond the Footprint | NURA
content.seo_description: Plan a kitchen appliance garage around appliance size, lifting and filling space, open doors and the worktop you still need. Start with the actual manuals.

hero.alt: Open charcoal countertop appliance cupboard with oak lining, a stored mixer and blender, and clear counter beside it

social_image.caption: A countertop cupboard stores disconnected appliances beside a separate worktop area. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: A kitchen appliance garage conceals countertop appliances behind cabinet doors, often in a cupboard that sits on the worktop. Plan it around more than the appliances' stored dimensions: record how you lift out a jug, remove a bowl, fill a reservoir and clean the parts. Establish where each appliance may be stored and used before choosing the cabinetry.
Separate storage from operation

An appliance fitting inside a cupboard does not establish that it can be used there. Read the exact model's instructions for storage, operating position, surrounding space and access. An open cabinet door or a pull-out shelf is not, by itself, permission to run the appliance in that location.
For example,
Dualit's toaster guidance

advises against keeping a toaster in an appliance garage or pantry-style cupboard, especially while in use. Check storage restrictions as well as operating instructions; do not reduce that advice to simply leaving the doors open. If a model is unsuitable for the proposed cupboard, give it a different permitted home and working position.

This is a cabinetry planning brief, not an approval of an appliance installation. Ask the designer to coordinate the chosen appliance instructions with the furniture and any proposed electrical work before the design is agreed.
Record the movement around the appliance

List the models you own or intend to buy, including their attachments. Measure the actual items and note which parts lift upward, slide forward or detach. Ask for the usable cabinet opening and interior dimensions rather than relying on the overall cupboard width.
Part of the task
What to record
Put away
Appliance footprint, cable and attachment positions, permitted storage conditions
Take out or fill
Jug, lid, bowl or reservoir movement; comfortable handling route
Clean and return
Where detached parts rest and how the interior can be reached

A photograph of a neatly arranged cupboard cannot show those movements. Check them with your own appliance, switched off and disconnected as its instructions require. A cardboard outline can help discuss the layout, but it does not replace appliance instructions or the cabinet supplier's specification.

Imagine a household using a compact blender every morning and a mixer only occasionally. They might prioritise an accessible cupboard position and nearby setting-down space for the blender, while considering separate permitted storage for the mixer. Moving a heavy appliance each time may change that preference. This is a hypothetical trade-off to discuss, not a recommended allocation for every household.

Show the proposed doors, adjacent drawers and the place where someone stands. Hinged doors occupy a different position from doors that fold or slide into pockets.

content.title: Kitchen Cookbook Display: Keep a Place for the Open Book
content.summary: Separate the closed cookbook collection from the book you are reading, with covers, spines and remaining counter space in view.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Cookbook Display: Covers, Spines and Reading Space | NURA
content.seo_description: Separate the cookbook you are using from the books you display. Compare covers and spines, support the books and leave room for the open volume and its stand.

hero.alt: Plum kitchen cabinetry with an oak cookbook shelf, supported closed books and one ochre cover facing out

children.text: A kitchen cookbook display needs two places: somewhere for the closed collection and somewhere to read the book you are using. Begin with your actual books, rather than buying a stand to complete a photograph. A cover facing the room and a recipe open on the counter take up different amounts of space.
Decide what the display should show

Set out a small group you genuinely want to keep nearby. Spines make titles visible in a row; a front-facing cover gives one book more visual attention while concealing what is behind it. Choose the arrangement around how you find a recipe as well as how it looks from the dining area.

In a hypothetical plum kitchen with an oak shelf, one ochre cover could connect with an ochre dining chair. The remaining books might stay spine-out, including a blue volume that introduces another colour. This is a palette idea, not a rule to colour-sort a collection or buy books as props. Keep the titles you reach for easy to identify.

Use your usual cookbook and, where available, the actual stand. Check the base, the open pages and the room to turn them. Do not assume the book occupies only the stand's footprint. Leave the preparation area you need available rather than filling the counter with a permanent display.

content.title: Kitchen Peninsula vs Island: What Happens at the Attached End?
content.summary: Compare the route past an attached end with a continuous worktop, cabinet junction and dining-facing finish.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Peninsula vs Island: The Attached-End Decision | Nura
content.seo_description: Compare a kitchen peninsula with an island through everyday routes, the cabinet junction and the dining-room view. Bring a clearer layout brief to Nura.

hero.alt: Terracotta kitchen peninsula joined to a rear cabinet run with an open end beside a timber dining table
hero.caption: A terracotta peninsula connects the kitchen worktop beside a timber dining area. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: A kitchen peninsula joins a wall or cabinet run at one end; an island stands separately. That attachment is the useful starting point for choosing between them. It removes a route past one end while connecting the worktop to the rest of the kitchen. Decide whether that connection helps your daily routine before treating either layout as the obvious choice for your room size.
Follow the route that the connection would close

On a room plan, mark the entrance, fridge and dining table. Trace one ordinary trip, such as taking breakfast from the fridge to the table while someone else prepares food. Draw the peninsula's attached end across that plan, then compare a freestanding island. Which way would each person actually go?

Consider a hypothetical room with a doorway near the proposed attachment and a table beyond it. A peninsula could send that breakfast trip around its far end. An island might keep the nearer route available, provided the complete layout leaves usable space there. In another room, a peninsula could deliberately separate passing traffic from the cooking area. The doorway positions change the answer; neither arrangement guarantees better flow.
Andrew James's layout discussion
likewise places household needs, doorways and through-traffic ahead of a standard room-size answer. Our
island measurement guide
develops the finished outlines and surrounding spaces once you have a promising arrangement.

A continuous worktop may suit a preparation routine that moves along the perimeter and onto the return. Ask what you would put on that connected surface and where the same task would happen with an island. More counter is useful when it has a job, rather than simply completing a shape.

Look beneath the junction too. If the design creates corner storage, identify what belongs there and how you would take it out. Compare the actual cabinet arrangement; do not assume that joining two runs automatically gives convenient storage. Our

content.title: Kitchen Cabinets to the Ceiling: More Storage or Just a Finished Top?
content.summary: Separate usable upper storage from the finished top line, then record the ceiling detail and access on your kitchen drawings.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Cabinets to the Ceiling: Storage or a Finished Top? | Nura
content.seo_description: Separate extra cupboards from a closed finishing band or an open gap. Plan what belongs up high, then resolve the ceiling detail on your kitchen drawings.

hero.alt: Ochre tall cupboards with a separate upper row beside an ash kitchen worktop and ivory ceiling
hero.caption: Ochre tall cupboards and an ash worktop run meet the room's ceiling and coving. Concept interior, Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Ochre tall cupboards with a separate upper row beside an ash kitchen worktop and ivory ceiling
social_image.caption: Ochre tall cupboards and an ash worktop run meet the room's ceiling and coving. Concept interior, Nura Interiors.

children.text: Taking kitchen cabinets to the ceiling can mean adding usable cupboards, closing the top with a finishing panel, or simply making the furniture appear taller. Decide which result you want before choosing the top line. A closed gap and extra storage are different purchases, even when they look similar from the kitchen doorway.

Start with two questions: what needs a home, and what would you like the wall to look like? Keeping those answers separate helps you discuss the cabinet interior and the room's proportions without assuming one must dictate the other.
Separate the cupboard from the finishing detail

Ask your designer to identify the cabinet box, doors and top finishing pieces on an elevation. A panel that closes the space above a cupboard should not be counted as accessible storage unless the agreed construction actually provides it. Equally, a line across a front view does not tell you whether it represents a door, a joint or a decorative detail.
Option
What you are choosing
What to confirm
Additional upper cupboard
An enclosed place for specific belongings
Internal space, opening and a suitable way to retrieve the contents
Closed finishing band
A visual connection between cabinet and ceiling
The proposed finish and whether the area has any access or storage function
Deliberate open gap
Visible wall above the furniture
Its appearance from the room and how that surface will be maintained

These are design options, not interchangeable installation instructions. A cornice is a top moulding; its appearance alone does not establish how the space behind it is built. Ask for the actual proposed detail rather than ordering from a reference photograph.

body_nodes.caption: Left to right: an upper cupboard, a solid finishing band and a deliberate open gap. Concept arrangements, Nura Interiors.

children.text: Give the upper space a real job

List the objects you intend to keep, their size and how often each is used. Then consider the person who will put them away and take them down. An empty rectangle marked 'storage' on a drawing leaves those everyday movements unresolved.

For a hypothetical household, mugs belong in the daily routine while a serving platter comes out for occasional meals. The platter is a reason to discuss extra storage, but it is not automatically a reason to place it at the top. Its weight, shape and retrieval need consideration. If it already has a suitable home in a
larder cupboard
, the remaining wish may be a cleaner-looking cabinet top rather than more shelves.

Keep frequently used belongings in positions that work for the people using the room. Do not make standing on a worktop or chair part of the plan. If access needs equipment, ask how suitable access and somewhere to keep it will be provided. Review the
drawers-versus-cupboards decision
before sending more daily objects upwards.
Draw the ceiling relationship across the whole wall

Include the window, coving, beams, tall units and worktop run in the same elevation. Compare the proposed top from the entrance and a dining seat. One continuous line may be your preference; another room may benefit from a deliberate break beside retained architectural features. Neither choice guarantees that a kitchen will feel larger.
The
Painted Kitchen Company's ceiling guide

highlights measuring the ceiling at several points and including cornice and installation space. Take that as a prompt for the measured survey and fitting discussion, not a transferable cabinet dimension. Ask who will confirm the finished room levels and resolve the top junction before manufacture.

Where cabinetry contains an appliance, have the supplier and installer check its actual installation and ventilation instructions. Do not treat a decorative gap as proof of compliant ventilation, or agree to close one without confirming its purpose.
Make the drawing and quotation describe the same choice

Request a written record identifying the usable upper cupboard, any non-storage finishing area, the door opening and the agreed treatment at the ceiling. Confirm which party measures, supplies the finishing pieces and completes the junction. If the proposal changes, update the drawing and specification together before approval.
Bring a wall photograph showing the ceiling, an inventory of the proposed upper contents and your current plan to a
Nura kitchen conversation
. They help connect storage needs with
bespoke cabinetry
and the room's architecture. Explore
Elm Park Road

for documented cabinetry context, and ask which relevant material or cabinet examples are available before visiting the showroom. The concept images here show alternative appearances, not measured construction details or a completed Nura project.

content.title: Dining Chair Colour: Tucked In and Pulled Out
content.summary: Compare the visible seat, back and frame in two room views, then connect your dining furniture choice with the kitchen palette.
content.seo_title: How to Choose Dining Chair Colour | Nura Interiors
content.seo_description: Compare dining chair colour tucked in and pulled out. Use a two-view checklist to consider the seat, back and frame beside your table, floor and cabinets.

hero.alt: Oak-backed chairs with blue seats beside a dark timber table and terracotta kitchen cabinets
hero.caption: Oak chair backs, blue seats and a dark table alongside terracotta cabinetry. Concept interior, Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Oak-backed chairs with blue seats beside a dark timber table and terracotta kitchen cabinets
social_image.caption: Oak chair backs, blue seats and a dark table alongside terracotta cabinetry. Concept interior, Nura Interiors.

children.text: To choose dining chair colour, compare the whole chair beside your table, floor and kitchen cabinetry. Look at it tucked in and pulled out: the seat, back and frame can contribute different amounts of colour in each position. Use that comparison to decide what you want to remain visible in the room.
Make a two-view record

Stand where you normally see the dining area, perhaps at the kitchen doorway. Take one photograph with the chair in its usual tucked-in position and a second from the same viewpoint with it pulled out. Include the table edge, floor and adjacent cabinetry in both views.

Record the surfaces you can actually see. A timber back may be prominent while its coloured seat is partly screened by the table. A fully upholstered back may leave a larger area of fabric visible. The result depends on the chair, table and viewpoint, so check your arrangement rather than assuming the seat disappears.

For a chair you have not bought, request images and dimensions of the exact model from its supplier. If a physical comparison is available, use it to check the relationship with the table. Keep any finish or fabric references with the photographs; a room photograph is a visual brief, not approval of an exact colour match.
Two blue chairs can make different statements

Imagine keeping an oak floor and a dark dining table while planning terracotta kitchen cabinets. One chair has a blue seat and an oak back. Another has blue upholstery across both seat and back. Both introduce blue, but the second puts it on a larger back surface, including the view from behind the table.

If your aim is to retain more visible timber beside the cabinets, compare the oak-backed option. If you want the chair backs to carry the blue accent, compare the upholstered-back option. These are different design intentions; neither is a universal rule for which colour looks best.

content.title: Kitchen Splashback Height: Choose Where the Surface Ends
content.summary: Compare the window, cupboard and open-wall stopping points, then record the finish line and measuring responsibility in your kitchen brief.

content.seo_description: Choose kitchen splashback height around the window, wall units and daily use. Compare finish lines, then record the coverage and measuring responsibility.

hero.alt: Pale stone splashback rising from a window sill to the underside of oak wall cabinets
hero.caption: Stone rising from the window sill to the oak cupboard underside. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Pale stone splashback rising from a window sill to the underside of oak wall cabinets
social_image.caption: Stone rising from the window sill to the oak cupboard underside. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Choose kitchen splashback height by deciding where the protective surface should finish on each wall, then have the actual dimensions confirmed for the chosen material and appliances. The underside of a wall cabinet, a window sill and a ceiling are different stopping points. A number on a product listing cannot choose between them for your room.
Start from the finished worktop

On a wall drawing, mark the finished worktop surface and the intended top edge of the splashback. Describe the height between those two lines, rather than giving an unexplained measurement from the floor. Include any upstand already planned: is the new surface sitting above it, replacing it or continuing the same material?

Keep the visible wall coverage separate from the supplier's final panel dimensions. Edge joints, returns, overlaps and fitting allowances need the selected product's instructions and the installer's agreement. For example,
Belling describes its own splashbacks
as having a visible height of 750mm. That is a product description, not a height to transfer to every kitchen.
Compare the stopping points

With wall cupboards, filling the gap to their underside gives the surface a clear boundary. On an open wall, decide whether you want a low band, a finish aligned with a window or shelf, or coverage continuing to the ceiling. Look at the whole elevation, including the exposed side edges and adjoining run.
Option
What to compare in the room
What to settle in the brief
Low upstand or band
More painted wall remains visible
Whether that coverage suits the sink, preparation and cleaning routines
To the cabinet underside
The surface fills the space framed by worktop and cupboards
How it meets any lower window sill or open section
To a shelf or window line
An existing horizontal feature becomes the stopping point
The top edge, reveal and side-return treatment
To the ceiling
The wall surface continues behind shelves or around openings
Extent, joints, access, fitting and the complete quoted scope

No option is automatically the right amount of protection. Explain where you wash, prepare food and use countertop appliances, then confirm the material and coverage with the supplier and installer. Include the wall beside the sink, not just the space directly behind the tap.
When the window and cupboards do not line up

Imagine a sink wall where the sill sits lower than the underside of the adjoining wall cupboards. A splashback kept level with the sill leaves a painted strip below the cupboards. A stepped top edge can fill that cabinet gap while staying beneath the window. Continuing the finish around the opening is another design option to draw, rather than assume.

For a homeowner who wants a quiet horizontal band, the first arrangement may be worth exploring. Someone who wants the surface to fill the cabinet gap may prefer the step. Compare both on the same wall drawing, with the same finish. Then ask how the change in level and exposed edge will be made, and whether the proposed coverage suits that sink area. Do not lower a hood or choose a wall material to preserve a decorative line. Give the designer and installer the exact hob and extractor model references, and have them check both installation manuals and the proposed wall build-up.
Bosch's installation guidance
explicitly notes that measurements and methods can vary by model. A general splashback-height suggestion does not establish an appliance clearance.

Ask for an elevation that shows the coverage on each run, including top and side edges, window reveals, any upstand and planned socket positions.

content.title: Choosing Placemat Colour? Put the Plate on First
content.summary: Compare the colour visible around your everyday plate, then judge the repeated settings in the wider kitchen palette.
content.seo_title: How to Choose Placemat Colour With Your Plates | Nura Interiors
content.seo_description: Choose placemat colour by comparing the border visible around your plate, then repeat the settings across your kitchen table. A practical colour-selection tip.

hero.alt: White plates on clay and olive rectangular placemats, with cutlery and glasses on a pale oak table
hero.caption: Clay and olive placemats framing matching white plates on pale oak. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: White plates on clay and olive rectangular placemats, with cutlery and glasses on a pale oak table
social_image.caption: Clay and olive placemats framing matching white plates on pale oak. Nura Interiors.

children.text: To choose placemat colour, put your everyday plate on each option first. Judge the colour and pattern still visible around it, then look at the complete table from the kitchen doorway. A mat you like on its own may contribute a very different amount of colour once the table is set.
Compare the visible border

Keep the plate, cutlery and mat size the same while comparing two colours. Add your usual glass and napkin too. If you change the shape, size and colour together, it becomes harder to identify which difference you prefer.

Look at the exposed edges rather than the covered centre. A patterned mat might lose its main motif beneath the plate, leaving only a striped or floral border. Decide whether that remaining detail gives you the effect you wanted. You do not have to match the mat exactly to either the table or the chairs.
What you see
What to compare next
The mat nearly disappears against the table
Try a lighter or darker option of the same size if you want a clearer outline.
The border feels more prominent than you intended
Compare a colour closer to the tabletop, or a less contrasting pattern.
The central pattern is hidden
Choose using the edge you can actually see, or try a different pattern layout.
Repeat the colour across the table

For example, imagine a pale oak table with white plates. Compare muted clay and olive mats using the same white plate. Both are possible starting points. Choose between the visible borders yourself rather than assuming that one colour must suit every oak table.
Next, imagine that border repeated at every seat. Where possible, lay out the full set before deciding. Step back to the doorway and compare it with the kitchen cabinets and
dining-chair colours
. Decide whether the mats should quietly repeat an existing colour or introduce a deliberate accent.

Check the real sample under the lighting you normally use for meals. A screen image is a starting point, not a promise of an exact colour match. Keep material suitability and cleaning requirements as separate buying checks against the product instructions.
Bring the setting into your kitchen brief
If you are planning the kitchen as well as its accessories, keep a doorway photo, your plate colour and shortlisted samples together. Use them when discussing the wider palette through
Nura's bespoke kitchen service
. The useful question is specific: should the dining table repeat the kitchen colours, or provide an accent of its own?

content.title: Kitchen Plinth Height Starts with the Finished Floor
content.summary: Separate the kickboard size from cabinet support height, then coordinate the floor, worktop and appliance arrangement on one section drawing.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Plinth Height: Coordinate the Floor and Cabinets | Nura Interiors
content.seo_description: Plan kitchen plinth height with the finished floor, cabinet supports, worktop and appliances. Separate board size from installed height before approving the design.

hero.alt: Recessed olive plinth beneath warm grey kitchen cabinets with an oak end panel and pale stone floor
hero.caption: Recessed olive plinth beneath warm grey cabinetry and an oak end panel. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Recessed olive plinth beneath warm grey kitchen cabinets with an oak end panel and pale stone floor
social_image.caption: Recessed olive plinth beneath warm grey cabinetry and an oak end panel. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Choose kitchen plinth height as part of the whole cabinet and appliance arrangement. Start from the finished floor level, agree the worktop height, then check the cabinet system and appliance requirements together. A stock kickboard dimension alone cannot tell you whether the finished kitchen will fit.

The visible plinth is the board across the bottom of the cabinets. In a kitchen supported on adjustable legs, it conceals those supports. Its height and its horizontal setback from the doors are separate decisions: a taller board does not automatically give your feet more room behind the door fronts.
Separate the board from the space it covers
Ask what a quoted plinth measurement describes. Is it the supplied board height, the distance from finished floor to cabinet underside, or the intended visible band once fitted?
Howdens' plinth catalogue
includes boards listed at 165 mm high. By contrast,
IKEA's METOD leg
is nominally 80 mm high, with a stated adjustment range of 75 to 95 mm. These are examples from different systems, not interchangeable specifications or a recommended range for every kitchen.
The board closes the visible gap; the cabinet support arrangement establishes the cabinet level. Confirm the actual system rather than changing a board dimension and assuming that the rest follows.

body_nodes.alt: Cabinet body and worktop above adjustable legs, with an olive plinth board separated in front
body_nodes.caption: Cabinet supports behind a removable plinth board. Parts shown schematically, not to scale. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Work backwards from the agreed worktop level

For a simple cabinet stack, the floor-to-worktop height includes the support zone, cabinet body and worktop. Any additional rail, profile or support layer must be accounted for in the actual section drawing.

As a hypothetical example only, a 720 mm cabinet body on a 150 mm support zone with a 20 mm worktop totals 890 mm. If the cabinet and worktop stay at those fixed levels, raising the finished floor by 10 mm reduces the height measured above the new floor to 880 mm. This arithmetic is not an installation specification or a recommendation for a particular person.
Agree the floor build-up and its reference level before confirming the cabinet setting-out dimensions. Ask the fitter how floor variations will be accommodated while keeping the cabinet run level.
DIY Kitchens' fitting advice
describes adjusting the feet to level its units before attaching the plinth.
Check the appliance arrangement before approving a low plinth

A low visible band may be your preference, but confirm that the chosen cabinet and appliance combination permits it. Check the exact appliance's installation height, door movement, ventilation requirements and future removal route. Do not infer a ventilation gap from a room image.
For a specific example,
DIY Kitchens' True Handleless Fitting Guide 2024
specifies a 160 mm plinth height to accommodate 820 mm-high integrated appliances beneath its horizontal worktop profile. That requirement belongs to that arrangement. It is not a rule for every
handleless kitchen
Put the height decision in the kitchen brief
Record together
What needs confirming
Finished floor and worktop levels
Which surfaces are the measurements taken from?
Cabinet, support and plinth details
What is supplied, what is adjustable and what is fitted to the surveyed floor?
Exact appliance models
Do the openings, door movement and required ventilation work with this cabinet section?
Plinth setback and access
Can you stand comfortably at the worktop, and how is the board removed for access?
Bring the proposed floor build-up, cabinet section, worktop thickness and appliance model numbers to a
bespoke kitchen discussion with Nura

. Ask for the agreed levels and any appliance-dependent exceptions to be recorded on the same drawing. That makes the plinth a coordinated design decision rather than a last-minute strip chosen to fill a gap.

content.title: Joinery Tender Packages: Make the Drawings and Schedule Agree
content.summary: Cross-check a furniture item across drawings, schedules and finishes, then keep tender updates traceable with a worked window-seat example.
content.seo_title: Joinery Tender Package: Drawings, Scope and Revisions | Nura
content.seo_description: Prepare a joinery tender package with matching drawings, schedules and finish references. Use a worked example to record open choices and issue changes clearly.

hero.alt: Window-seat bookcase drawings and material references arranged on a dark timber table
hero.caption: Window-seat bookcase concept, drawings and material references. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Window-seat bookcase drawings and material references arranged on a dark timber table
social_image.caption: Window-seat bookcase concept, drawings and material references. Nura Interiors.

children.text: A useful joinery tender package gives each workshop the same identified drawings, item list, specification and enquiry instructions. Before sending it, cross-check one furniture item across those documents. If the elevation shows drawers but the schedule says shelves, resolve that difference rather than leaving each supplier to interpret it.

For architects and interior designers preparing a residential enquiry, the immediate decision is what the workshop is being asked to price, and on what information. You can start a conversation while choices remain open, provided their status and pricing basis are clear. This guide focuses on the package you send, rather than the quotations you receive.
Start with the furniture, then identify the files

List the rooms and pieces included in the enquiry. Give each piece a stable reference, such as J03 for a window-seat bookcase. Use that reference on its drawing, schedule row and relevant finish information. A description such as living-room joinery is useful context, but it does not establish whether a window seat, shelves and adjacent panelling are all included.

Keep two records distinct. An item schedule describes the furniture: its location, arrangement, material references and scope. A document issue register identifies the files sent: their titles, revisions, issue date and recipients. One tells the workshop what to price; the other records which information it received. Use the naming system already agreed by your project team.
Check one item across the package

In this hypothetical example, J03 is a window-seat bookcase beside an existing fireplace. Drawing J-203 revision B shows cupboard doors below the seat and open shelves above. The item schedule describes the same arrangement and references finish F02. The dimensions are still subject to the agreed survey and technical-development process; this example is not a measured design.

body_nodes.caption: Hypothetical J03 enquiry cross-check

Then repeat the check for the remaining pieces. Include relevant sections and junction details where they explain the work being priced. A reference image can communicate atmosphere or a finish direction, but it cannot replace the written description of construction, fittings and scope. Keep images and finish codes linked to the item they concern.
Describe open choices without hiding them

Suppose the client has not chosen the seat finish. State the common basis you want priced, identify the unresolved decision and name the role responsible for confirming it. If an alternative is requested, ask for it separately so it remains distinguishable from the base proposal. Do not insert an arbitrary allowance simply to fill a blank.

Check that scope boundaries are equally clear: drawing development, site measurement, samples, manufacture, delivery, fitting and making good. Identify relevant services and adjacent work, and ask the appointed specialists to confirm their responsibilities and technical requirements. A joinery lighting recess, for example, does not establish who supplies or connects the lighting.

Explain the information stage honestly. An early budget enquiry may rely on stated assumptions; a developed tender requires a more defined basis. Ask the workshop what further information it needs for the response you are seeking. Do not label incomplete information as manufacture-ready.
Issue changes as a traceable update

Now imagine the client selects finish F03 for J03. Keep the furniture item reference J03. Update the affected drawing and schedule revisions, identify the new finish reference and record the change in Issue 02 or the project addendum. Identify which earlier files are superseded, retain them in the project record and tell tenderers which set is current.

Send the same relevant scope update to all tenderers and request acknowledgement. Record the response reference and clarify whether the change affects their return date. If drawings and written information conflict, raise the discrepancy with the project team. Do not assume a document automatically takes precedence; the appointment and project documents need to establish how conflicts are resolved.

Identify the package issue and item references the workshop should price.
State the return format, requested date and contact for questions.
Ask for assumptions, exclusions and proposed alternatives to be identified clearly.
Describe known access, delivery and site constraints, and identify information still to be confirmed.
State which design, survey, sample and technical approvals will be agreed before manufacture.
Issuing tender information is a pricing step, not by itself a release to manufacture. Confirm the later approvals and responsibilities for the actual appointment. Once proposals arrive, use our
bespoke joinery quote comparison
to review the scope behind each figure.
Prepare a focused Nura project conversation
Bring the current drawings, item schedule, finish references, issue list and unresolved questions to a
Nura professional project conversation

. Include the project location, stage, budget parameters and dates that matter. Explain the design priorities too: for J03, whether the seat is used daily, what the shelves need to hold and how the new furniture relates to the retained room.

Nura architectural joinery
and the
documented Westover Road joinery
, then
discuss your drawings and scope
. Confirm the services and responsibilities for your particular project in writing. The useful next step is a coherent brief that the design team and workshop can discuss against the same references.

content.seo_title: Value Engineering Bespoke Joinery: Compare the Changes | Nura
content.seo_description: Compare bespoke joinery changes against storage needs, design priorities and the full revised price. Use a practical example to record trade-offs and approvals.

hero.alt: Oak cabinet-front options with framed doors on the left and flat slab doors on the right
hero.caption: Framed and slab cabinet-front concepts for comparing appearance. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Oak cabinet-front options with framed doors on the left and flat slab doors on the right

children.text: Value engineering bespoke joinery starts by asking what the furniture must still do after a proposed change. Write down those needs, compare the alternative against them and obtain a revised price for the complete affected scope. A simpler-looking cabinet is not evidence of a saving, and a lower quotation does not explain what the client is giving up.

For architects, interior designers and developer teams reviewing a residential joinery package, the useful decision is whether a particular alternative offers an acceptable balance of cost, use and appearance. This guide uses an unpriced hypothetical dining-room cabinet to show how to make that judgement visible.
Agree what you are trying to preserve
SAVE International describes value methodology

as analysing functions while balancing performance, quality, safety and cost. Applied to a joinery discussion, begin with the purpose of the furniture rather than a list of expensive materials to replace. This is a practical comparison aid, not a formal value-methodology study.

Imagine a cabinet fitted into a dining-room alcove beside an open-plan kitchen. The household wants plates behind closed doors, a drawer for cutlery and a clear route around the dining table. The designer wants the door divisions to sit comfortably with the adjacent kitchen. Record those priorities separately: concealed storage, accessible cutlery, circulation and the visible composition.

Then ask which priorities are essential and which the client is willing to reconsider. If a decorative frame is central to the agreed room, removing it changes more than a detail. If it was only one possible expression of the brief, a simpler front may be worth exploring. The client needs to see that difference before accepting a new sum.
Compare one proposed change at a time

Keep the original proposal identifiable and ask for alternatives separately. Otherwise a new front, different interior and narrower cabinet can arrive as one lower figure, making it difficult to understand which change produces which effect.

children.text: Alternative
Retain
Trade-off
Confirm
Simplify a framed front to a slab front
Closed storage and the agreed cabinet arrangement
The door detail changes; its relationship with the kitchen needs review
Revised elevation, proposed finish and construction, and actual revised quotation
Replace the cutlery drawer with a shelf
The outer cabinet and closed storage
Cutlery storage changes; a tray elsewhere may be needed
A workable place for the actual contents, revised interior and net price difference
Explore a standard-width cabinet with fillers
A closed cupboard within the alcove
Usable width, door proportions and filler lines may change
Surveyed fit, clearances, finishing and fitting scope, and complete installed quotation

None of these alternatives is automatically cheaper or technically equivalent. Ask the supplier and relevant project specialists to confirm suitability for the intended contents, fittings and location. A visual comparison can help with appearance; it cannot establish load capacity, durability or installation requirements.
Name a reduced requirement honestly

In the cabinet example, removing the drawer does not remove all storage, but it does remove the intended cutlery arrangement. The client may happily accept a tray in another location. Record that as an agreed change to the requirement, rather than saying nothing has been lost.

Likewise, omitting an entire cabinet may be a sensible budget decision if the household no longer needs it. It is a scope reduction. Keeping the distinction clear allows the client to choose a smaller brief without confusing it with an alternative that fulfils the original brief. Do not reject a useful reduction simply because it is not like-for-like.
Ask for the total effect, not a material-price guess

Request the original and revised amounts on a consistent basis, with the affected work identified. Ask whether the change alters drawing development, samples, manufacture, delivery, fitting or making good. Check the treatment of VAT and any separately priced work. Use the
bespoke joinery quote comparison
when the figures cover different scopes.

Before calling the difference a saving, establish whether redesign, changed adjacent work or existing order commitments add costs elsewhere. Ask for any effect on the programme and who will confirm it. Do not assign a percentage saving, cancellation charge or lead time without a project-specific response. An option can remain worth considering while its net effect is still unconfirmed.
Review materials without a universal hierarchy

Veneer is not a single specification, and neither is solid timber. If a substitution is proposed, identify the actual material, substrate where relevant, edge detail, finish and intended use. Ask the supplier to explain how the complete construction meets the requirements. Do not approve an unnamed alternative just because its colour resembles the original.

Look at the proposed finish sample alongside the retained kitchen or room materials, under the lighting that matters to the project. Record the sample reference and what it represents. A sample helps judge appearance and texture; it does not prove the performance of a complete cabinet. Our
solid wood or veneer guide
introduces the material decision without making one label a universal winner.
Record the decision before the instruction changes

For the hypothetical cabinet, give the proposal a reference such as VE01 and connect it to the existing furniture item reference. Record the original arrangement, proposed alteration, retained requirements, accepted compromises, quotation reference and outstanding questions. Separate visual/client acceptance from technical confirmation and the authority to instruct the change under the actual appointment.
Status: proposed, awaiting information, accepted or rejected, with the date and responsible role.
Evidence: revised drawing, finish reference, quotation and relevant technical response.
Consequences: affected adjacent work, confirmed cost basis and any programme impact.
Instruction: who is authorised to proceed, which documents change and who receives the update.
A discussion or attractive render is not by itself authority to manufacture. Confirm the project-specific approval route and update the affected drawings, schedule and order information. Our
joinery tender package guide

explains keeping those references consistent. If work has already been ordered or started, establish the actual commitments before instructing an alternative; there is no universal last safe date for a change.
Prepare a focused Nura conversation
Bring the current drawings, original quotation, proposed alternatives and a short ranked list of priorities to a
Nura professional project conversation

and

children.text: Kitchen plate display ideas work better when you decide which plates need to come down at mealtimes. Keep frequently used crockery easy to retrieve; give favourite decorative pieces a setting that does not depend on those everyday plates staying in place. Sort by use, then choose the display

Put your plates into three groups: used at most meals, brought out occasionally, and kept mainly for display. Record the quantity and largest diameter in each group. A serving platter can be both useful and decorative, but it still needs a way out of its display without moving half the collection.

Try this arrangement

and

content.title: Joinery Schedules: Give Every Cabinet a Clear Identity
content.summary: Turn a room list into identifiable furniture items, clear quantities, finish references and open decisions, with a worked cupboard record.
content.seo_title: Joinery Schedule: Cabinet Items, Quantities and Scope | Nura
content.seo_description: Build a clear joinery schedule with item references, quantities, finishes and open decisions. Follow a cupboard example and prepare a useful project brief.

hero.alt: Oak kitchen and dining cupboards with different storage arrangements beside a concept schedule and finish samples
hero.caption: Cupboard layouts, item-record concept and finish references. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Oak kitchen and dining cupboards with different storage arrangements beside a concept schedule and finish samples
social_image.caption: Cupboard layouts, item-record concept and finish references. Nura Interiors.

children.text: A joinery schedule should let the project team identify each piece of built-in furniture, understand what it includes and find the information still needed. Start with a stable item reference and room location, then connect that entry to its drawings, finishes, internal arrangement and quantities. A room list saying kitchen, dining room and study is a useful starting point, but it does not yet describe the furniture to be discussed or priced.

For architects and interior designers preparing a residential brief, the practical aim is a clear item record. This guide concerns a schedule of furniture and specifications, not a production timetable. It uses two hypothetical cupboards to show why matching finishes do not necessarily mean identical items.
Start with the furniture, then attach the room

Walk through the room list and name the separate fitted elements. A dining room might contain an alcove cupboard and a low serving cabinet; those are two items even if they share one room and one timber finish. Decide how the team will identify each one on a plan and in the schedule. Use the same references wherever those items appear.

For example, call a tall kitchen crockery cupboard J01 and a low dining-room cupboard J02. These are example identifiers, not an industry coding standard. Keep each reference stable as the design develops. If a room name changes, update the location rather than casually renaming every furniture item. If one item is removed or replaced, record that change so an old drawing does not quietly reintroduce it.

Record where the item sits within the room as well as its room name: beside the kitchen doorway, or within the dining alcove. The reference should allow someone reading the schedule to find the right object on the relevant plan. Avoid relying on descriptions such as cupboard on left, which depend on where the viewer is standing.
Separate a repeated type from a physical item

A type describes a repeatable arrangement; a physical item is an occurrence in a particular location. Before grouping cupboards into one type and quantity, establish what is genuinely the same: dimensions, construction, internal layout, finish, fittings and relevant interfaces. A common external appearance is not enough to establish interchangeability.

In our example, J01 stores everyday plates on adjustable shelves, while J02 has a cutlery drawer above closed storage. Both may use the same proposed oak finish, but their internal arrangements differ. Record them separately while those requirements are being developed. Do not turn two different cupboards into a quantity of two identical units simply because their doors look related.

State the counting basis too. Is a scheduled quantity one complete cupboard, one cabinet module or one door front? A clear description makes the number meaningful. Reconcile the count with the plan; do not count an elevation of the same object as another piece of furniture.
Build one useful item record

The following is an unpriced discussion example for J02. It shows the information to capture, not a measured specification or permission to manufacture. Keep the schedule readable and refer to the appropriate drawings or detailed specification rather than squeezing every construction detail into one cell.

body_nodes.caption: Hypothetical J02 dining cupboard: fields for a developing item record

children.text: Field
Example entry
Resolve or reference
Identity and count
J02, dining alcove, one complete cupboard
Locate J02 on the current plan; confirm the complete assembly included
Use and internal arrangement
Cutlery drawer above closed crockery storage
Record actual contents and the proposed drawer/shelf arrangement
Size and interfaces
Dimensions and junctions remain to be developed
Identify survey and drawing references; resolve skirting, wall and adjacent-work details
Materials and finish
Proposed oak exterior, shared finish reference F01
Define which surfaces use F01; identify the sample and any different internal finish
Fittings and open decisions
Handle and drawer fitting selection pending
Name who will provide the missing information and record the next action

The useful record makes incompleteness visible. Dimensions to be developed is more honest than inserting a nominal width that nobody has checked. Give an unresolved field an owner and next action in the project record. A blank cell leaves readers to guess whether information is missing, not applicable or included elsewhere.
Use shared references without hiding differences

A finish register can describe a shared material or sample once, with individual items referring to it. Explain where that finish applies: visible doors, end panels, shelving or interiors. A note saying oak throughout may be interpreted differently by different readers. If J01 has a painted interior and J02 a timber interior, make the distinction explicit.

Keep appearance decisions connected to use. For J01, the plate sizes and shelf arrangement matter to the storage brief. For J02, the cutlery contents and drawer access matter. An attractive common door finish does not resolve either requirement. Ask the relevant supplier to confirm suitable construction and fittings for the intended use; a schedule entry alone cannot establish technical performance.

Identify handles, runners, lighting or other fittings with appropriate references as they are selected. Keep product references current and record meaningful alternatives separately. Do not bury a different fitting or finish inside a general note and assume that everyone will price or supply the same thing.
Make scope boundaries and revisions readable

State which associated elements are included in the item or described elsewhere: a top, lighting, glass, internal organisers or connections to adjacent work. Identify interfaces that need coordination without assuming that a furniture supplier is responsible for every surrounding trade. Agree the actual appointment and information responsibilities with the team. The
RIBA Plan of Work
provides a wider framework for discussing project stages and responsibilities; this example schedule is not a prescribed RIBA form.

Give the schedule an identifiable issue and keep changes traceable. If the client adds a cutlery drawer to J02, update the internal-arrangement entry and the associated drawing reference. Record the revised information and who needs it. For coordinating a schedule with the wider drawing package, use our
joinery tender package guide
. For the separate decision about what a drawing review authorises, read
kitchen shop drawing reviews
Choose a format the team can keep current

A spreadsheet or another agreed structured format can work if the people receiving it can read the references, follow changes and distinguish current information. A PDF issue can preserve a record of what was sent, but agree how updates will be communicated. Software does not resolve inconsistent item names or missing scope.

Before issuing the schedule, follow one item from its plan location through the record to its drawing, finish reference and unresolved questions. Then compare the quantities across the package. If different documents disagree, ask for clarification rather than selecting whichever description looks most complete. When prices arrive, our
guide to comparing joinery quotations
helps separate what is included in each offer.
Bring an item-led brief to Nura
For a
professional project discussion

, bring the room list, marked-up plans, current item schedule, finish references and open questions. Explain the relationship you want between the kitchen and nearby furniture, as well as what each cupboard must hold. J01 and J02 may need a coherent external palette while working differently inside.
Explore
Nura architectural joinery
and the
documented Westover Road joinery
, then ask the studio to confirm the development and supply scope available for your project. The cupboards in this guide are hypothetical and are not a description of that completed project.
Discuss your joinery item list with Nura
to clarify which information and decisions should come next.

If different documents disagree, ask for clarification rather than selecting whichever description looks most complete. When prices arrive, our  guide to comparing joinery quotations  helps separate what is included in each offer.

Bring an item-led brief to Nura

For a  professional project discussion , bring the room list, marked-up plans, current item schedule, finish references and open questions. Explain the relationship you want between the kitchen and nearby furniture, as well as what each cupboard must hold. J01 and J02 may need a coherent external palette while working differently inside.

content.summary: Resolve each filler by its purpose, installed width and the storage access behind the front.

hero.alt: Blue-grey pantry beside a plaster wall with a narrow matching filler strip, an open door and adjacent oak worktop
hero.caption: Blue-grey pantry and a matching strip at the wall junction. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Blue-grey pantry beside a plaster wall with a narrow matching filler strip, an open door and adjacent oak worktop
social_image.caption: Blue-grey pantry and a matching strip at the wall junction. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Kitchen filler panels close planned gaps beside cabinetry, but the space they occupy can also let doors, handles and internal storage work properly. Decide what each gap must do before choosing the narrowest-looking strip. A neat front elevation is only useful if you can still reach what is inside.
Identify which panel the drawing means

A filler closes a gap, for example between a cabinet run and a wall. An end or cover panel finishes an exposed cabinet side. An appliance filler may close part of an appliance housing. These are different jobs, even when the supplier makes the pieces from matching material.
IKEA's cover-panel range

describes matching or contrasting exposed cabinet sides. That is a finish decision, whereas a wall filler also needs its position and width resolved. Your drawing may need both an end panel and a filler, so ask for each to be identified separately rather than treating every narrow line as the same component.
Separate the supplied size from the installed width
A catalogue dimension tells you the size of a supplied piece. It does not establish the correct finished gap for your room.
Howdens lists filler panels
in different sizes and finishes; the particular cabinet arrangement still needs checking.

Ask the supplier or fitter to confirm the installed width against the selected door, hinge, handle and adjacent wall. Record projecting skirting, architraves or window boards, as well as changes in the wall along the panel's height. Where the panel must be scribed to follow the wall, agree how that affects the piece to order and its finished face. Confirm cut-edge treatment for the actual material instead of assuming every panel can be finished in the same way.
Check access behind the front
The important question is not just whether the outer door opens. Can the internal drawers extend, and can the items you intend to store be taken out?
DIY Kitchens' wall-gap advice
shows how handles and tall-unit access affect the answer. Its dimensions describe particular arrangements, not a universal clearance for every kitchen.

Imagine a household choosing a tall pantry for cereal containers and heavy serving dishes. A slim filler looks appealing on the elevation, but the proposed internal drawers also need the pantry door out of their path. Before approving the narrower line, ask the supplier to demonstrate the opening relationship on the specification or drawing. If more room is required, compare a different hinge or door arrangement with changing the cabinet run. This is a design choice to resolve, not a gap to disguise later.
The same thinking belongs in
corner-storage planning

. Check the actual configuration rather than borrowing the allowance from a different corner cabinet. For appliances, keep the exact model's installation and ventilation requirements alongside the housing drawing; a matching panel is not permission to close a required opening.
Give each filler a short drawing note
Use a location reference so the conversation ends with a decision you can find again. The following is a preparation guide, not a set of installation dimensions.

Job to resolve
Ask to have confirmed

bespoke kitchen brief
: storage priorities, front proportions and the way the room is used.

and ask what support is available for resolving those details. The useful outcome to request is a clearly identified panel and an agreed opening arrangement, rather than a universal filler width.

content.title: Kitchen Utensil Holders Need Room Above the Rim
content.summary: Compare the filled pot, the space used by utensil heads and the drawer storage around it.

content.seo_description: Compare a kitchen utensil holder with your actual spoons, whisk and turners. Check the loaded outline, removal space and nearby drawer before choosing the finish.

hero.alt: Terracotta utensil pot with wooden spoon, turner, whisk and plum spatula beside clear worktop and an open walnut drawer
hero.caption: Terracotta utensil pot, clear worktop and a walnut drawer for occasional tools. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Terracotta utensil pot with wooden spoon, turner, whisk and plum spatula beside clear worktop and an open walnut drawer
