children.text: A kitchen utensil holder takes up more room once the tools are in it. Spoon heads, whisks and turners can spread beyond the rim, so compare the filled arrangement with your working surface before choosing a pot for its colour or base size alone.
Look at the whole outline

Start with the tools you want on the worktop, not every tool you own. In a suitable utensil pot you already have, arrange that selection and look from above and from the room entrance. Notice how far the heads spread, whether they hide the splashback detail you like, and what surface remains for your usual chopping board or preparation task.

This is a way to prepare a shopping brief, not a rule about how many tools every household needs. Photograph the arrangement with the rest of the counter visible. An empty product photograph cannot show how your own whisk or broad turner will sit.
Compare access as well as appearance

Take out and return each chosen tool. If the handles bunch together or you must move several others to reach one, compare a different opening or a smaller selection. Check the maker's intended use and care instructions rather than assuming a decorative vase or a particular material is suitable.

Question to answer
Possible next choice
The filled outline

Move some tools into a drawer instead of enlarging the pot

Bring the pot into the kitchen palette

Suppose your regular cooking uses a wooden spoon, a turner and a whisk, while the rolling pin comes out occasionally. Compare those everyday tools in the pot and give the rolling pin a deliberate drawer position. The useful decision is what stays visible and what storage must work around it.

Then judge the pot's finish beside the retained worktop, cabinet fronts and tool handles. A contrasting colour may be welcome, but it still needs to work when the pot is filled. Keep that photograph with your
drawer-organisation brief
Discuss your kitchen with Nura
using the counter photograph, tool list and preferred finishes. Ask what support is available for connecting this small detail with the wider

content.title: Kitchen Sink Drainers: Compare the Space in Use and Cleared
content.summary: Compare the drying surface, remaining preparation space and storage needed for a removable rack.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Sink with or without a Drainer? | Nura Interiors
content.seo_description: Choosing a kitchen sink with or without a drainer? Compare fixed boards, removable trays and over-bowl racks while drying dishes, clearing up and storing them.

hero.alt: Two walnut kitchen sink areas, one with a steel draining board and the other with a removable dark tray holding plates and a mug
hero.caption: Two sink-area arrangements with an integral steel draining board and a removable counter tray. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Two walnut kitchen sink areas, one with a steel draining board and the other with a removable dark tray holding plates and a mug
social_image.caption: Two sink-area arrangements with an integral steel draining board and a removable counter tray. Nura Interiors.

children.text: A kitchen sink with a fixed drainer reserves a drying surface beside the bowl. A sink without one leaves you to choose another drying arrangement. Neither choice removes the need to plan where hand-washed items go. Compare the area while dishes are drying, after they are put away, and with any removable rack stored.
Start with what stays out of the dishwasher

List the items you actually wash by hand, following their makers' care instructions. A few mugs need a different arrangement from a large pan, serving platter and several containers. Note whether these items wait to dry while someone prepares the next meal. Having a dishwasher does not answer that question by itself.

For a hypothetical weeknight, most plates go into the dishwasher but a pan and a wooden board remain. If they stay beside the sink through breakfast preparation, a removable tray still occupies that counter during breakfast. Its empty appearance in a product photograph does not establish how much preparation space your household will have.
Compare three drying arrangements

An integral draining board stays part of the sink when it is empty. A removable counter tray can reveal worktop when it is moved, but needs a suitable place to go. An over-bowl rack uses space above the bowl instead. Compare the complete arrangement, including any rack needed to support your dishes, rather than treating every draining surface as interchangeable.
Arrangement
While dishes are drying
When cleared
Integral draining board
The fixed surface beside the bowl is occupied
The draining board remains in the sink's footprint
Removable counter tray
The tray and dishes occupy adjacent worktop
Worktop is available after the tray is cleaned, dried and stored as instructed
Compatible over-bowl rack
The rack covers part of the bowl opening
The opening is available after removal, with storage still needed for the rack

Use the size of your current drying arrangement as a starting point for a plan sketch. Add the pan or platter that makes the arrangement difficult, then show your usual chopping board nearby. A paper outline helps compare occupied areas; it cannot prove accessory fit, support or drainage.
Check the model, the side and the water path
Franke's UK sink selection guide

distinguishes sinks that need a particular left- or right-hand drainer version from reversible models. It also asks buyers to check the specified cabinet width. Confirm those details for the exact sink, alongside its worktop and installation requirements.

For a separate tray, establish whether it collects water for emptying or directs it into the sink, and how it is cleaned. For an over-bowl accessory, check the maker's compatibility, support and use instructions. If you are considering grooves or a recessed area in the worktop, ask the fabricator whether the proposed detail is suitable for that specific surface and how it will work. Do not assume that a groove or a loose rack provides a complete drying arrangement.
Bring both views to the kitchen discussion

Photograph the sink area in use and cleared. Bring the hand-washed item list, proposed sink and accessory details, and a sketch showing the drying area beside your preparation space. Record where a removable tray or rack would be stored. These inputs make the appearance and daily-use trade-off specific.
If bowl configuration is still undecided, compare
single and double kitchen sinks
separately. Explore
Nura bespoke kitchens
, then
discuss your sink area and kitchen brief
with the studio.

content.title: Gloss or Matt Kitchen Wall Tiles? Look at What They Reflect
content.summary: Use the window, evening lights and viewing position to choose the reflective role of your tiled wall.
content.seo_title: Gloss or Matt Kitchen Wall Tiles? Reflections and Care | Nura
content.seo_description: Choosing gloss or matt kitchen wall tiles? Compare reflections from your prep area and dining seat, separate sheen from texture, and check product-specific care.

hero.alt: Paired plum-coloured kitchen wall surfaces with bright window reflections on the left and a softer matt appearance on the right
hero.caption: Gloss and matt plum-coloured wall surfaces beside a pale counter and walnut cabinetry. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Paired plum-coloured kitchen wall surfaces with bright window reflections on the left and a softer matt appearance on the right
social_image.caption: Gloss and matt plum-coloured wall surfaces beside a pale counter and walnut cabinetry. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Choosing gloss or matt kitchen wall tiles? Start with what you want the wall to reflect. A gloss surface can introduce distinct highlights; a matt surface usually gives a softer reflection. Neither label tells you how easily a particular tile cleans. Compare actual samples in the planned position, then check the care guidance for each product.
Give the reflection something specific to reveal

Hold samples upright against the intended wall and keep them secure. Where possible, compare the same colour, size and layout in both finishes. If the products differ in colour, relief or shape, note those differences rather than attributing the whole effect to sheen.

Look from your normal preparation position and from the dining seat or doorway. Notice whether you see a window shape, a bright strip or a softened patch of light. Repeat with the evening lights you intend to use. A sample lying flat on a showroom counter cannot show the same view as your wall.
View
Notice
Record
Daylight at the wall
Where the window reflection falls
The position where you like or dislike the highlight
Intended evening lighting
Whether a lamp or light strip appears in the tile
Which light and viewing position create the effect
Beside cabinet and worktop samples
Whether the wall becomes the main reflective surface
Which surface you want to draw attention to
Separate sheen, relief and care

A flat matt tile and a rippled gloss tile change two things at once. Look at surface relief separately and ask the supplier how to clean that exact product. Marks being less noticeable does not establish stain resistance or remove the need for cleaning.
Ask for the product reference, approved cleaning method and any special restrictions.
Original Style's Living fixing guide
gives particular lustre ranges their own cleaning instructions, a useful reminder that a finish name is not a universal care specification. Follow the guidance for the tile you actually select.
Choose the role of the wall

For example, imagine an open-plan kitchen where a pendant is visible from the dining table. If its reflection makes the tiled wall feel busier than you want, compare the matt option from that seat. If you enjoy a lively highlight, retain gloss on the shortlist. The observation, rather than a rule that small kitchens need gloss, gives you a reason for the choice.
Keep the
tile layout
and
grout colour

consistent while deciding on sheen. Bring wall photographs, the tile references and cabinet/worktop samples to a kitchen design conversation. Note which reflections you want to keep and which you want to soften, and ask Nura what material examples are available before a showroom visit.

content.title: Joinery Samples and Mock-Ups: What Does Your Approval Cover?
content.summary: Decide what each sample or mock-up represents, then separate accepted choices from the information still needed.
content.seo_title: Joinery Samples and Mock-Ups: What Each Can Show | Nura
content.seo_description: Compare joinery samples, physical mock-ups and digital views, then record what is accepted, what remains open and who can authorise the next step.

hero.alt: Green finish panel and oak reference beside a partial cabinet corner model
hero.caption: Surface references and a partial cabinet model. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Green finish panel and oak reference beside a partial cabinet corner model
social_image.caption: Surface references and a partial cabinet model. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Joinery samples and mock-ups should answer a named question, not stand in for approval of the whole cabinet. Before accepting one, agree what it represents: a finish, a particular junction, a full-size element or a digital view. Record what you have reviewed and what still needs evidence or a decision.

For architects and interior designers coordinating residential joinery, that distinction keeps a material choice connected to the furniture it belongs to. A client can like a timber finish while the return edge, internal arrangement or opening movement remains unresolved. A general note saying “sample approved” leaves those separate decisions unclear.
Start with the question the sample must answer

Ask the team to complete one sentence: “We need this sample or mock-up to review...” The answer might be the finish beside retained flooring, the meeting of a door face and return edge, or the arrangement of a whole cabinet front.

Then agree what must be represented for that review. Is the finish on the intended material and profile? Does the corner include both adjoining parts? Is the full-size item a working component, a visual model or a sample installation? Identify substitutions and omitted parts rather than assuming the name of the sample explains them.
The following distinctions are practical descriptions for a project conversation. Agree the actual deliverable with the supplier; different teams may use the same word for different things.

body_nodes.caption: Choose the representation around the question; agree the actual review scope

children.text: Representation
Question it can help address
What to keep separate
Physical finish sample
How does this represented surface look beside the proposed materials?
The whole item, unrepresented edges and any technical requirements not demonstrated.
Physical corner or section mock-up
How do the included parts meet, and does that visible detail express the design intent?
Missing adjoining work, whole-room fit and any movement not actually shown.
Full-size element or item
How does the represented arrangement read at its stated scale?
Whether it is functional, which fittings are included and what remains outside its agreed review purpose.
Digital view
How does the proposed arrangement relate visually to the room?
Physical surface, touch and operation, plus site and product information requiring separate confirmation.
Choose a useful detail, rather than a larger model by default
A complete prototype is not automatically the right answer to a small unresolved question.
Woodcraft's Making Mock-Ups guide
includes partial physical models used to examine selected relationships between parts. The useful principle is to choose the representation around the question.

For a cabinet meeting a shelf, a defined corner or section might help the team discuss the visible junction. If the question concerns a whole door arrangement, a corner alone may leave too much unseen. Ask what further evidence is needed, rather than calling the smaller model a complete test.

A digital view has a different role. It may communicate the proposed room composition, but a convincing image does not establish what an actual surface feels like or demonstrate a physical opening movement. If operation is the question, identify the working arrangement and information needed with the appointed specialists.

body_nodes.alt: Green cabinet face, oak return and shelf shown together in a partial corner model
body_nodes.caption: Front edge, return, shelf and pull in a cabinet-corner concept. Nura Interiors. This is not a measured construction detail.

children.text: Follow one sample through a decision

Consider a hypothetical dining cabinet, J04. Finish sample S12 represents the proposed green front surface. The client accepts that finish direction, but the return-edge profile is still open. A corner mock-up is then requested to discuss the junction between the green front, oak return and adjacent oak shelf.

Keep those decisions distinct. The finish note can identify S12 and say what appearance has been accepted. The junction note can name the unresolved profile and the revised detail needed. If the mock-up has no working door or hardware, record “opening movement not demonstrated” rather than treating the assembled corner as evidence of operation.

The result might be: finish direction accepted for the represented surface; edge profile awaiting review; movement information outstanding; manufacture not instructed. This is a discussion example, not a measured Nura project or a prescribed approval procedure.
Keep the sample linked to the current information

Record the item, sample identifier, version, related drawing issue and review purpose together. Add the observation, unresolved points, named respondent and next action. Identify who is reviewing appearance, who provides the relevant technical information and who may instruct the next step under the actual appointment.
Our
kitchen drawing review guide
explains why accepting one aspect does not release every other aspect. Use the

content.body:
Joinery samples and mock-ups should answer a named question, not stand in for approval of the whole cabinet. Before accepting one, agree what it represents: a finish, a particular junction, a full-size element or a digital view. Record what you have reviewed and what still needs evidence or a decision.

For architects and interior designers coordinating residential joinery, that distinction keeps a material choice connected to the furniture it belongs to. A client can like a timber finish while the return edge, internal arrangement or opening movement remains unresolved. A general note saying “sample approved” leaves those separate decisions unclear.

Start with the question the sample must answer

Ask the team to complete one sentence: “We need this sample or mock-up to review...” The answer might be the finish beside retained flooring, the meeting of a door face and return edge, or the arrangement of a whole cabinet front.

Then agree what must be represented for that review. Is the finish on the intended material and profile? Does the corner include both adjoining parts? Is the full-size item a working component, a visual model or a sample installation? Identify substitutions and omitted parts rather than assuming the name of the sample explains them.

The following distinctions are practical descriptions for a project conversation. Agree the actual deliverable with the supplier; different teams may use the same word for different things.

    

Choose a useful detail, rather than a larger model by default

A complete prototype is not automatically the right answer to a small unresolved question.  Woodcraft's Making Mock-Ups guide  includes partial physical models used to examine selected relationships between parts. The useful principle is to choose the representation around the question.

For a cabinet meeting a shelf, a defined corner or section might help the team discuss the visible junction. If the question concerns a whole door arrangement, a corner alone may leave too much unseen. Ask what further evidence is needed, rather than calling the smaller model a complete test.

A digital view has a different role. It may communicate the proposed room composition, but a convincing image does not establish what an actual surface feels like or demonstrate a physical opening movement. If operation is the question, identify the working arrangement and information needed with the appointed specialists.



Follow one sample through a decision

Consider a hypothetical dining cabinet, J04. Finish sample S12 represents the proposed green front surface. The client accepts that finish direction, but the return-edge profile is still open. A corner mock-up is then requested to discuss the junction between the green front, oak return and adjacent oak shelf.

Keep those decisions distinct. The finish note can identify S12 and say what appearance has been accepted. The junction note can name the unresolved profile and the revised detail needed. If the mock-up has no working door or hardware, record “opening movement not demonstrated” rather than treating the assembled corner as evidence of operation.

The result might be: finish direction accepted for the represented surface; edge profile awaiting review; movement information outstanding; manufacture not instructed. This is a discussion example, not a measured Nura project or a prescribed approval procedure.

Keep the sample linked to the current information

Record the item, sample identifier, version, related drawing issue and review purpose together. Add the observation, unresolved points, named respondent and next action. Identify who is reviewing appearance, who provides the relevant technical information and who may instruct the next step under the actual appointment.

Our  kitchen drawing review guide  explains why accepting one aspect does not release every other aspect. Use the  joinery schedule  to connect the sample reference to the correct furniture and finish locations.

For colour viewing in the room, use the separate  kitchen colour sample guide . Keep photographs as a record of the review, with the physical reference identified; do not let a photograph silently replace the agreed sample.

Bring the unresolved question to Nura

Bring the current elevation, item and sample references, material direction and the junction or arrangement you cannot yet judge. Explain what has already been accepted and what remains open.

Explore  Nura architectural joinery  and our  information for architects and designers , then  discuss the brief with the studio . Ask what sampling or mock-up deliverable is appropriate and included for your particular proposal, and how its review connects to the next design decision.

content.title: Kitchen Tap Spout Reach: Match the Drawing to the Sink
content.summary: Connect the horizontal tap dimension with the bowl and mounting point, then check height and movement separately.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Tap Spout Reach: Match Tap and Sink | Nura Interiors
content.seo_description: Understand kitchen tap spout reach, outlet height and lever movement. Put the tap drawing and sink plan together before approving the mounting arrangement.

hero.alt: Plan and side views of a kitchen tap and oval sink, with arrows marking reach and outlet height and a not-to-scale label
hero.caption: Plan and side views showing a tap's reach and outlet height beside a sink. Not to scale. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Plan and side views of a kitchen tap and oval sink, with arrows marking reach and outlet height and a not-to-scale label
social_image.caption: Plan and side views showing a tap's reach and outlet height beside a sink. Not to scale. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Kitchen tap spout reach is a horizontal measurement, but the right choice depends on where the tap sits relative to the inside of your sink. Put the tap and sink drawings together before choosing by appearance. Then check outlet height and moving parts separately: a taller tap is not necessarily a longer-reaching one.
View the tap and sink diagram at full size
. The diagram is not to scale; use the selected products' drawings for dimensions.
Read the endpoints, not just the number
Kohler's measuring guide

describes reach from the spout-base centre horizontally to the water stream, and distinguishes it from height to the highest point. For the tap you are considering, use the reference lines on its own drawing. A dimension to the front of the spout is not automatically a dimension to the outlet centre.

Do not measure along the curve of a swan-neck spout. Find the horizontal dimension and its endpoints. Keep overall height and outlet height distinct too; the highest part of an arch does not tell you how much space is below the outlet.
Put the mounting point on the bowl plan

On a plan, identify the proposed mounting centre, the actual bowl opening and the outlet's position using the product drawing. Include the distance between the mounting point and the inside edge of the bowl. The overall sink size alone leaves that relationship unresolved.

For a replacement, imagine keeping an existing tap hole while changing to a tap whose outlet projects further forward. The bowl has not moved, but the outlet's position relative to it has. Compare both arrangements on the same plan rather than assuming the new tap's similar silhouette means a similar fit. If replacing only a spout, ask the supplier to confirm compatibility with the existing tap; reach alone does not establish that the component fits.

There is no single reach number in this guide for every sink. Nor does a plan prove the path of a real water stream or guarantee splash-free use. Ask the supplier and installer to confirm the proposed combination before holes or final fabrication details are approved.

Check the movement that a still photograph hides
A lever's travel matters beside an upstand or window. For example,
Franke's Active L model 115.0653.298
has a forward-only lever. That is a feature of that model, not a rule for all side-lever taps. Check the selected tap's movement against the actual surroundings.

If considering a pull-out spray, distinguish its docked position from use with the hose extended. Follow its installation requirements, including the space needed below the counter. A longer hose does not remove the need to check the original mounting arrangement.
Bring a coordinated sink brief

Keep the tap and sink model references, drawings and proposed mounting position together. Add photographs of any window, shelf or upstand, and identify who will confirm the final arrangement. Connect this with your
sink-bowl choice
and
drying arrangement
, so the tap is considered as part of daily use.

Bring that record to a Nura kitchen design conversation. It provides a concrete starting point for discussing the sink area alongside cabinetry and worktop decisions. Ask which relevant examples are available before a showroom visit.

content.title: Style Glass Kitchen Cabinets with the Doors Closed
content.summary: Look through the closed door before adding more objects, then open it to check how the cabinet works.
content.seo_title: Styling Glass Kitchen Cabinets: Look Through Closed Doors | Nura
content.seo_description: Style glass kitchen cabinets around the door frame and the pieces you use. Compare the closed-door view, shelf lines and everyday access before adding more.

hero.alt: Closed blue glazed cabinet doors framing oak shelves, a blue jug, cream plates and cups, with Nura Interiors credit
hero.caption: Closed glazed cabinet doors, oak shelves and blue and cream crockery. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Closed blue glazed cabinet doors framing oak shelves, a blue jug, cream plates and cups, with Nura Interiors credit
social_image.caption: Closed glazed cabinet doors, oak shelves and blue and cream crockery. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Start styling glass kitchen cabinets by looking through the closed doors, not just arranging objects on an open shelf. The door frame is part of the display. Put the pieces you want to keep there in place, close the doors and look from a normal position in the room. Then open them again to check that the arrangement works for daily use.
Notice what the frame hides

A jug can look well placed on an open shelf but sit partly behind a horizontal door rail when the cabinet is closed. Before adding another object to fill the apparent gap, try the jug in another suitable existing position. Keep it stable and easy to retrieve; the view is only one part of the decision.

Look at the shelf lines too. Do they sit behind the door rails, or create a second set of lines across the glass? Neither arrangement needs a universal verdict. Note which view you prefer with your actual contents, rather than judging the empty cabinet alone. A photograph taken straight on can help you explain that preference.
Notice
Try
Keep

Can you take out and return the things you use without shifting the display each time? Keep useful pieces in positions that work for their users. Our
plate-display tip
considers what happens when daily plates leave the shelf;
open-shelf styling
covers the separate question of objects displayed without a door frame.

This is an arrangement exercise, not permission to alter the cabinet. Follow its product instructions. Ask the supplier to confirm any proposed shelf-position or fitting change rather than adjusting supports or glazing to suit a photograph.
Bring the closed-door view into the brief

For new cabinetry, keep a contents list and mark the preferred view on the cabinet elevation. Include the door divisions and proposed shelf positions. If you are considering different glazing, look through the actual samples with representative objects behind them; do not choose from a picture of an empty door alone.

Bring those references to a Nura kitchen design conversation alongside your cabinet colours and adjacent worktop materials. They make the storage and display wishes concrete. Ask which relevant samples or examples are available before visiting the showroom.

content.title: Whole-Home Joinery: One Supplier or Separate Room Packages?
content.summary: Compare one defined joinery proposal with separate room packages, then make shared design decisions and handovers explicit.
content.seo_title: Whole-Home Joinery Supplier: Compare Room Packages | Nura
content.seo_description: Choosing a whole-home joinery supplier? Compare one combined proposal with separate room packages, shared finishes, coordination and installation responsibilities.

hero.alt: Kitchen and hall cabinetry with related timber details seen across a dining space
hero.caption: Related timber details across kitchen and hall cabinetry. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Kitchen and hall cabinetry with related timber details seen across a dining space
social_image.caption: Related timber details across kitchen and hall cabinetry. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Choosing a whole-home joinery supplier starts with deciding what belongs in the package. Compare one proposal covering the defined rooms with an alternative that divides them between named suppliers. Make the shared design decisions and coordination responsibilities visible before judging which arrangement suits your project.

For homeowners working with an architect or interior designer, the brief should explain what each room needs and who connects the packages. One supplier does not automatically mean one contract, identical finishes or management of the whole building project. Several suppliers do not automatically mean an unconnected interior.
Group the rooms around their actual needs

Start with the furniture you need, rather than a supplier's list of room categories. In a hypothetical home, the kitchen needs cabinetry arranged around cooking and appliances. Hall storage must accommodate coats, shoes and bags. The dressing room needs an internal layout suited to the clothes and accessories its users own.

Those rooms might share a timber direction or a restrained door detail without sharing the same internal construction, fittings or storage arrangement. Decide which relationships matter to you: a view from the hall into the kitchen, a repeated handle finish, or a deliberate change of character upstairs.

Now compare two options for this hypothetical home. In the first, you ask one supplier to propose the kitchen, hall and dressing-room joinery. In the second, you retain a kitchen supplier and ask another to propose the hall and dressing-room package.
Put the two options on the same room map
Use a marked-up plan alongside a short record such as this. Replace the descriptions with the actual furniture and shared decisions in your project.

body_nodes.caption: Compare the same hypothetical rooms under two proposed package groupings

Dressing room

This map defines what you are asking suppliers to consider. It is not a complete furniture schedule or a substitute for their proposals. Once the grouping is clear, the
joinery quotation guide
helps you compare the work behind the prices.
Give shared finishes a clear purpose
Keep the relationship specific. K-F1 identifies the retained kitchen timber and H-F2 the proposed hall finish. The client wants a related warm timber character, not an exact match.

A decision note could read: “Design lead to record the reviewed relationship between K-F1 and H-F2, the client's accepted direction and any differences still open. Each supplier to identify the finish and surfaces included in its proposal.” The note connects the design decision to the two packages without assigning technical approval authority. With one supplier, ask which cross-room review its combined scope includes. A common finish name alone does not guarantee a particular match.
Our
sample and mock-up guide
explains how to define what a reference represents and what remains unapproved. Apply that distinction to the shared details without assuming that one accepted surface approves every room.
Name the handovers as well as the suppliers

Ask who develops each package's information and who coordinates the interfaces with the architect, builder and relevant trades. A supplier might cover cabinetry design and fitting without taking responsibility for adjacent stone, lighting or building work. Confirm the actual arrangement rather than assigning that role from the company name.

Discuss the rooms' readiness and access against the proposed programme. If the hall must remain usable while other work continues, explain that requirement. Ask how a change in one package will be communicated to the other and whether any shared decisions must be resolved first. Supplier count alone cannot establish an earlier completion date.

Identify the contacts for delivery, installation, snagging and later queries too. Confirm which services and terms apply to each package; do not infer one warranty or a single remedial process from a combined quotation.
Use the room map to shape the enquiry

Compare the actual offers against the room map and the coordination you need. If a kitchen appointment is already established, make its boundaries explicit when discussing the remaining rooms. If all rooms are still being developed, ask what a combined proposal would cover. Keep any unresolved responsibility visible before committing.
Then use the
tender package guide
to organise the information issued for that agreed scope.

content.summary: Compare the visible rim and exposed worktop edge, then confirm the exact sink, surface and mounting detail before cutting.

content.seo_description: Compare undermount and inset sinks by the edge you see, the worktop construction and the approved fitting detail. Keep the exact products together before cutting.

hero.alt: Paired closeups of a stainless undermount bowl below a stone edge and an inset sink with its metal rim above the worktop
hero.caption: Undermount bowl below a finished stone edge, beside an inset sink rim above the worktop. Nura Interiors.

social_image.caption: Undermount bowl below a finished stone edge, beside an inset sink rim above the worktop. Nura Interiors.

children.text: An inset sink sits in the worktop from above, with its rim visible on the surface. An undermount sink is fixed below, leaving the worktop edge visible around the bowl. Choose the relationship you prefer, then confirm that the exact sink and worktop permit it before approving a cut-out.
Compare the junction you will see
Franke's installation overview
distinguishes these arrangements from flushmount installation, where the sink rim sits level with the worktop. Flushmount is a separate detail, not another name for undermount.

Look at the proposed sink edge from above and in section. An inset rim can provide a visible outline; an undermount exposes the worktop's cut edge. Ask to see the actual detail rather than assume every inset has a broad rim or every undermount looks identical.

Consider how you would clean that junction, following the selected products' care guidance. A preference for wiping across an uninterrupted surface does not establish material compatibility, and an undermount still has a sink-to-worktop joint.
Find out what the worktop actually is

Imagine two kitchen proposals both described as having a laminate worktop. One uses laminate over chipboard; the other specifies compact high-pressure laminate. The label alone cannot settle whether your preferred sink mounting is permitted.
Polyrey's Compact HPL manual

permits drop-in and undermount resin or metallic sinks within its specified system, subject to the manufacturer's instructions. That permission does not approve every compact laminate, every sink material or a chipboard-backed product.

Give the sink supplier and worktop fabricator both product references. Ask them to confirm the compatible arrangement, including support, sealing and the exposed edge. Do not treat adding sealant as an answer to an unresolved compatibility question.

content.title: Joinery Snagging and Handover: Keep Open Items Traceable
content.summary: Connect installed joinery observations, unresolved finish decisions and care information to a clear follow-up record.
content.seo_title: Joinery Snagging and Handover: Record Open Items | Nura
content.seo_description: Plan a joinery snagging and handover record with clear item references, open finish questions, follow-up evidence and the care information owners need.

hero.alt: Hall cabinet with oak doors, a pale interior and a closer view of the open door edge
hero.caption: Hall cabinet context and door-edge detail for a joinery record. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Hall cabinet with oak doors, a pale interior and a closer view of the open door edge
social_image.caption: Hall cabinet context and door-edge detail for a joinery record. Nura Interiors.

children.text: A joinery snagging and handover record should connect each observation to a particular cabinet, the information it is being reviewed against and the next agreed action. Keep an unanswered design question, a reported repair and a checked outcome distinguishable. A photograph marked “done” cannot explain which of those has happened.

For architects, interior designers and clients reviewing fitted furniture, the useful outcome is a record the project team can follow after the walk-through. Pair it with relevant product and care information, rather than treating the snag list as the whole handover pack.
Locate the component and the reference

Start with the room, furniture item and particular part: “hall unit J08, right-hand door, lower outside corner” is more useful than “hall joinery”. Use the same item reference as the current drawings or
joinery schedule
, alongside a plain-language location.

Take a context photograph to locate the part and a closer view to show the observation. Date the record and identify the drawing issue, finish reference or other agreed information relevant to the question. Record what you can see without guessing its cause. If a surface is still protected or a cupboard cannot be accessed, say what has not been reviewed.

Keep observations that need different responses separately traceable. A concern about a door finish and a missing care sheet may involve the same unit, but receiving a document does not resolve the finish question.
Separate the observation from the decision
An apparent difference needs a clear comparison basis. Ask which surface the accepted sample represents, whether the current drawing records that choice and whether a later change was agreed. Our
samples and mock-ups guide
explains why accepting one finish or detail does not approve every part of the furniture.

Record an unresolved selection as a decision requiring a response, rather than quietly treating it as either an accepted finish or an agreed repair. Likewise, do not turn a newly requested feature into unfinished work without checking the agreed scope. The appointed project team should establish the appropriate response and authority for the actual appointment.

Describe concerns about normal operation without prescribing an adjustment. Do not force a component, remove hardware or carry out specialist testing to complete a list. Ask the relevant installer or specialist to assess anything outside the agreed review scope.
Follow one hall unit through close-out

Consider a hypothetical hall cabinet, J08. A small surface mark is visible at the lower outside corner of its right-hand door. Separately, the client asks whether its internal finish should match the outside. Sample F12 was accepted for the exterior doors, but the available record does not settle the interior finish. The client also needs care information for the installed surfaces.
Avoid a single entry saying “finish wrong, rectify”. A useful record separates the questions:

body_nodes.caption: Separate records for one hypothetical hall cabinet

children.text: Record
Next response to request
Evidence to retain
J08 right-hand door, lower outside corner: visible surface mark
Joinery contractor to assess the marked area and confirm the proposed response, without assuming the cause or repair
Dated context and close views, relevant finish reference and the agreed response
J08 interior finish question, with dated location photographs
Design lead to identify the agreed interior selection or record the decision still required

Completion report and a separate dated review of that action

These are discussion records, not findings from a Nura project. The first response might clarify an existing agreement or reveal a decision still needed. It does not automatically establish a defect, a change instruction or permission to alter the cabinet.
Make closure a separate event

When someone reports an action complete, preserve that report and arrange the relevant review. State what was checked, by whom, when and against which original observation or agreed action. Keep the earlier photographs and add dated follow-up evidence where useful.

If the requested care sheet arrives, that document item can be recorded as received while the finish decision remains open. For the surface mark, a contractor's completion report should be followed by the agreed review of that same corner. Record what is visible and any remaining concern, rather than assuming that a report of completion proves acceptance. If an agreed physical action is reviewed, describe its actual outcome instead of replacing the original entry with “all satisfactory”. Record remaining access restrictions or questions explicitly. A closed action should not silently close unrelated concerns on the same cabinet.
Assemble information for everyday use

Alongside the open-action record, ask for the information applicable to the installed joinery: identified finishes and where they occur, relevant hardware or product references, supplied operation and care guidance, and the agreed contact for later queries. Ask which drawings or other records describe the completed scope, particularly where agreed changes occurred.

Confirm what is available, what is still requested and who will supply it. Do not substitute a generic cleaning recommendation for guidance appropriate to the actual finish. Where separate suppliers are involved, keep their contacts and scope identifiable, as discussed in our
whole-home supplier comparison

architectural joinery
project, bring drawings, finish references and an example of the handover information you need.
Discuss the scope with Nura
, including installation, completion review, care information and follow-up responsibilities for the proposed appointment.

content.title: Built-In Oven Height: Make the Measurement Unambiguous
content.summary: Name the point measured above the finished floor, then relate the actual oven and open door to its users and nearby surface.
content.seo_title: Built-In Oven Height from the Floor: What to Measure | Nura
content.seo_description: Separate oven size from mounting height. Record the finished-floor reference, measurement endpoint, exact model and open-door arrangement before fixing the cabinet design.

hero.alt: Open black oven in olive tall cabinetry beside a pale worktop, with a marker pointing to the finished floor
hero.caption: Olive oven cabinet with an open door beside a pale worktop and a finished-floor marker. Concept arrangement, not an installation drawing. Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Open black oven in olive tall cabinetry beside a pale worktop, with a marker pointing to the finished floor
social_image.caption: Olive oven cabinet with an open door beside a pale worktop and a finished-floor marker. Concept arrangement, not an installation drawing. Nura Interiors.

children.text: Built-in oven height from the floor is a different measurement from the height of the appliance itself. Before comparing positions, name the point you are measuring to: the bottom of the oven, its controls or a particular shelf. Then relate that point to the finished floor, the people using the oven and the space in front of its open door.
Olive oven cabinet with an open door beside a pale worktop and a finished-floor marker. Concept arrangement, not an installation drawing. Nura Interiors.
View the oven arrangement at full size
. The floor marker identifies the lower reference only; confirm the upper measurement endpoint on the selected model and cabinet drawing.
Give the height a clear reference

On a cabinet elevation, mark the top of the finished floor and the proposed oven position. Label the housing support or appliance-bottom line using the selected model's drawing, and distinguish it from the controls and shelf positions. An unexplained number beside a tall cabinet leaves too much open to interpretation.
The finished-floor line is not the top of the plinth. Include any floor finish still to be installed, and ask who confirms that level before the cabinetry is finalised. Our
kitchen plinth guide
considers the related cabinet and floor decision.
Keep the oven's outer dimensions separate from its required housing opening and its proposed position above the floor. Matching one measurement does not establish the others.
Use the actual model and door
Bosch's UK installation guide

says installation methods and measurements vary by model. Use the selected appliance's current instructions for the housing, ventilation and installation requirements, rather than transferring clearances from another oven.
The
Bosch manual 9001771067_A for HBF113BS0.
, for example, says a tall-unit installation must allow accessories to be easily removed. That is a useful access question, not a universal mounting height.
Look at the door open as well as closed. A drop-down door and a different mechanism change the arrangement in front of the cabinet.
NEFF's B54CR71N0B
has a sliding-away door; that feature belongs to that model and does not establish how another oven will work in your room.
Put the users and landing surface on the plan

Imagine two regular cooks comparing one oven in a tall unit. Aligning its controls with neighbouring cabinet lines might look appealing, but one person may prefer another position for seeing the shelf and taking a dish out. Record both people's needs instead of selecting a height from the cabinet appearance alone.

On the room plan, show the actual door's open position, where someone would stand and the intended surface for setting a dish down. Discuss the relationship between them, including anything occupying that surface during cooking. A sketch identifies questions; it cannot prove comfortable reach or safe handling.
